explanations.explanation: That's the one. The king "…ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles, to be brought in and read to him." (Esther 6:1). Xerxes, the king in this story, picked the records. I think that's some of the most sleep-proof reading material around.

Close, since it's a book of some kind, but that's not what the text says. The king ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles (Esther 6:1). Nothing in this scene says anyone reached for the Law. This is a record of what happened in the kingdom, and that matters in a minute.

A prophet's scroll would make for some heavy bedtime reading, but it isn't in this scene. The text says the king ordered "…the Book of Records, the Chronicles…" (Esther 6:1). That was the book he wanted, and what's inside it changes the whole night.

Not quite, friend. The record says the opposite: Mordecai "…had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the king’s entrance, when they had conspired to assassinate King Xerxes." (Esther 6:2). Mordecai was the one who blew the whistle. He wasn't in on the plot.

Right. The record says Mordecai "…had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the king’s entrance…" (Esther 6:2). Those two were the ones who had conspired to assassinate the king. Mordecai exposed the plot, and it was all written down.

Yep. The king asks what honor Mordecai received, and the attendants reply, "Nothing has been done for him…" (Esther 6:3). Mordecai saved the king's life, and the thank-you card never got written. I think the king is about to fix that.

If only. The attendants say, "Nothing has been done for him…" (Esther 6:3). Mordecai exposed a plot against the king, and nobody had given him a thing for it. The answer is the exact opposite of plenty.

That would be a nice ending for Mordecai, but not yet. The attendants tell the king, "Nothing has been done for him…" (Esther 6:3). So far Mordecai has no honor at all for saving the king. The king is not happy to hear it, I bet.

That's him. The attendants answer, "Haman is there, standing in the court." (Esther 6:5). He'd just walked in to ask the king to hang Mordecai. Of every person who could be standing there right now, it's him. The timing is unreal.

Hathach was a eunuch the king had assigned to serve Esther (Esther 4:5), but he isn't in this scene. The attendants say, "Haman is there, standing in the court." (Esther 6:5). It's Haman at the door, and his errand is the one that makes this scene so tense.

Esther isn't out in the court here. The attendants say, "Haman is there, standing in the court." (Esther 6:5). Esther does come up at the end of the passage, where the text mentions the banquet she had prepared (Esther 6:14). So the one waiting in the court is Haman.

That's right. The text says Haman "…had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him." (Esther 6:4). He came with his request already in hand. Meanwhile the king has Mordecai on his mind too, just for a very different reason.

It's true, friend. The text says Haman "…had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him." (Esther 6:4). He had come to ask the king for exactly that.

You got it. The text says Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?” (Esther 6:6). He heard “…the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” and figured it was him. That sets up the surprise.

It's actually true. The king asks what should be done for the man he is delighted to honor, and Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?” (Esther 6:6). So Haman figured the honor had his name on it. That's the setup for the surprise.
Yes, the robe is one "…the king himself has worn…" (Esther 6:8). Haman didn't ask for a nice new robe off the rack. He wanted the king's own robe. Haman was aiming high.
Right, it's a horse "…on which the king himself has ridden…" (Esther 6:8). It also wears a royal crest on its head. Haman is describing a very fancy day for the honored man.
That word isn't in Haman's plan. He asks for a robe "…that the king himself has worn…" (Esther 6:8). What matters to him is that the king wore it, not who sewed it.
Nothing about shopping here. Haman asks for a robe the king has worn and a horse the king has ridden (Esther 6:8). Worn and ridden are the words in his plan.

That word isn't in Haman's plan. He asks for "…a royal robe that the king himself has worn and a horse on which the king himself has ridden…" (Esther 6:8). The words are worn and ridden. The king's own things are what make the honor big.

explanations.answer: One of the king's most noble princes
explanations.explanation: That's it. Haman says, "Let the robe and the horse be entrusted to one of the king’s most noble princes." (Esther 6:9). That prince dresses the honored man and parades him through the city square. Haman is picturing a very classy parade.

explanations.answer: The captain of the royal guard
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a captain here. Haman says the robe and horse should be "…entrusted to one of the king’s most noble princes." (Esther 6:9). A prince is the one who dresses the man and leads the parade. That's a big job for a noble.

explanations.answer: One of the queen's own attendants
explanations.explanation: Haman doesn't bring the queen's staff into this. He says the robe and horse should go to "…one of the king’s most noble princes." (Esther 6:9). That's who dresses the honored man and parades him. Haman is picking someone with a lot of rank for the job.

Actually, it's the opposite. Haman's plan has the prince "…proclaiming before him, ‘This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!’…" (Esther 6:9). So someone announces it the whole way. Haman wanted the whole city square to hear it.

That's right. In Haman's plan the man is paraded "…through the city square, proclaiming before him, ‘This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!’…" (Esther 6:9). There's no quiet ride in this plan. Someone is announcing it the whole way.

That's the twist. The king says, "Take the robe and the horse to Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate." (Esther 6:10). Haman walked in with a plan to hang Mordecai. Now he's the one carrying out the honor for him.

Memucan was one of the king's advisers, who spoke up back in Esther 1:16, but he isn't the man being honored here. The king tells Haman to take the robe and horse to "…Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate." (Esther 6:10). This honor is for the man who exposed the plot against the king.

Hegai was the eunuch in charge of the women (Esther 2:3), but he isn't in this scene. The king names "…Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate." (Esther 6:10). Mordecai is the one whose good deed was sitting unrewarded in the records.
Not a chance. The king tells Haman, "Do not neglect anything that you have suggested." (Esther 6:10). Every piece of the plan has to happen. The king wants it all done.
Right. The king says, "Do not neglect anything that you have suggested." (Esther 6:10). The robe, the horse, the parade and the announcement all stay in. Haman doesn't get to cut a single step.

That's it. Haman "paraded him through the city square, crying out before him, 'This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!'" (Esther 6:11). He's the one who has to say it. I think that line had to taste strange coming out of his mouth.

The text doesn't say anything about a decree. Haman is crying out before him, “This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!” (Esther 6:11). That announcement is what he does along the way.

No gifts are mentioned in this scene. Along the parade route, Haman is "crying out before him, 'This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!'" (Esther 6:11). His job is the shouting, and he does it all through the city square.
Yes, "…Mordecai returned to the king’s gate." (Esther 6:12). After the parade, he went back to his spot. The text doesn't tell us what he was thinking, so I won't guess too loudly.
It's true, friend. The text says, "…Mordecai returned to the king’s gate." (Esther 6:12). That's where the king had said he was sitting. The parade ended and Mordecai went back to the gate.
That's the word. Haman "…rushed home, with his head covered in grief." (Esther 6:12). He had thought the honor was his. Then he cried it out for Mordecai and rushed home hurting.
Ashes aren't mentioned in this verse. It says Haman "…rushed home, with his head covered in grief." (Esther 6:12). Grief is the word the text gives.
Oil isn't what the text says. Haman "…rushed home, with his head covered in grief." (Esther 6:12). Grief is the word the text uses for how he went home.

explanations.answer: He will surely fall before Mordecai
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his advisers tell him, "…surely you will fall before him." (Esther 6:13). Haman had told them everything that happened, and that's the word he got back. Friend, that is a hard word to hear.

explanations.answer: Mordecai will soon fall before him
explanations.explanation: That's backwards. Zeresh and the advisers say Haman won't prevail against Mordecai, and tell him, "…surely you will fall before him." (Esther 6:13). It's Haman who is told he'll fall. Mordecai isn't the one in trouble in that sentence.

explanations.answer: The king will forget Mordecai by morning
explanations.explanation: They don't say that. They tell Haman, "…surely you will fall before him." (Esther 6:13). The king had just honored Mordecai in the middle of the city square, so forgetting him sounds unlikely to me. Their words are about Haman's downfall.

Yes. They say, "Since Mordecai, before whom your downfall has begun, is Jewish, you will not prevail against him…" (Esther 6:13). Their words point to Mordecai being Jewish as the reason. Haman's own household is telling him it's not going his way.
That's not the word they use. They say Mordecai "is Jewish" and that Haman "…will not prevail against him…" (Esther 6:13). Jewish is the word in the verse. It's what Zeresh and the advisers point to.

Egypt doesn't come up here. Zeresh and the advisers say Mordecai "is Jewish" and that Haman "…will not prevail against him…" (Esther 6:13). The word in the verse is Jewish. That's what they use to warn Haman.

That's where he goes. "…the king’s eunuchs arrived and rushed him to the banquet that Esther had prepared." (Esther 6:14). They didn't even let the conversation wrap up. Haman went from one big moment straight to another.

Not this time. The eunuchs "…rushed him to the banquet that Esther had prepared." (Esther 6:14). The gallows were built for Mordecai, but they aren't where Haman is headed here. He's off to Esther's banquet.
The text sends him somewhere else. The king's eunuchs "…rushed him to the banquet that Esther had prepared." (Esther 6:14). So Haman is heading to Esther's banquet. The throne room isn't mentioned.
